Data Models, Architecture and the ER Model

Chapters 2 & 3 of Elmasri & Navathe (7th ed.). Exercises 2.1–2.5, 2.14. Each topic below opens with its theory; the exercise topics give every assigned question with a full solution behind the Solution button. Questions marked must-do match past end-sem and quiz questions.

The story of this topic

A data model supplies the concepts, a schema describes one database in those concepts, and the state is the data at one moment. The three-schema architecture separates what users see, what the data means, and how it is stored. Data independence means you can change one level without rewriting the level above it. The part ends with the core of the ER model, which Topic 3 covers in full.

How the exercises are solved

Every assigned exercise, in textbook order. Each solution is written the way the Moodle keys are: assumptions with reasons, every step shown, and the final answer in an Answer box. Start with the exercises tagged ★ Must-do; they match past end-sem and quiz questions.

What is inside

    1  Data models, schemas and instances

    Theory recap

    Data abstraction and data models

    Definition: Data abstraction

    Suppressing the details of data organization and storage and highlighting the essential features, so that different users can perceive data at their preferred level of detail.

    Definition: Data model

    A collection of concepts that can be used to describe the structure of a database: its data types, relationships and constraints. Most data models also include basic operations for retrievals and updates, and increasingly concepts for dynamic behaviour (user-defined operations such as COMPUTE_GPA on a STUDENT object; stored procedures in relational systems).

    Watch out

    “Data model” is the set of concepts (e.g. the relational model), not a particular database’s description. The description of one database (“the marketing data model”) is its schema.

    Categories of data models

    CategoryConcepts / audienceExamples
    High-level (conceptual)Close to how users perceive data: entities, attributes, relationships. Good for communicating with non-technical users.ER model (Ch. 3), EER model (Ch. 4).
    Representational (implementation)Understandable by end users but not far from how data is organized in storage; hide many storage details yet can be implemented directly. Use record structures, so also called record-based.Relational model (most widely used); legacy network and hierarchical models; the object data model (ODMG) as a higher-level implementation model.
    Low-level (physical)How data is stored as files: record formats, record orderings, access paths (search structures such as indexes and hashing). Meant for computer specialists.Index/file organization descriptions (Ch. 16–17).
    Self-describingThe data description is stored with the data values instead of in a separate schema.XML; key-value stores and NOSQL systems.

    Schema, schema diagram, database state

    Definition: Database schema

    The description of the database, specified during database design and not expected to change frequently. A displayed schema is a schema diagram; each object in it (STUDENT, COURSE, …) is a schema construct.

    A schema diagram shows only some aspects: record types and data-item names, some constraints. It does not show data types, the relationships among files, or most constraints (“CS majors must take CS1310 before the end of their sophomore year” is hard to draw).

    Definition: Database state (snapshot)

    The data in the database at a particular moment: the current set of occurrences (instances). In a given state each schema construct has its own current set of instances (the STUDENT construct contains the set of student records). Every insert, delete or modify changes one state into another.

    • Defining a new database: only the schema is given to the DBMS; the state is the empty state.
    • Loading the initial data gives the initial state; every update then gives a new state; at any time there is a current state.
    • The DBMS is partly responsible for ensuring every state is a valid state: one that satisfies the structure and constraints in the schema, so the schema must be designed with utmost care.
    • The schema is stored in the catalog as meta-data.
    • Schema = intension; database state = extension of the schema.
    • The book prefers “instance” for individual records; “database instance” is sometimes used for a state.
    Definition: Schema evolution

    Changing the schema after the database is operational because requirements changed, e.g. adding Date_of_birth to STUDENT. Most modern DBMSs support schema-evolution operations while the database is running.

    Schema (intension)State (extension, snapshot)
    WhatDescription: record types, data items, types, constraintsActual data at one moment
    ChangesRarely (schema evolution)On every insert/delete/update
    SpecifiedAt design time, in the DDLBy loading and updating data (DML)
    StoredIn the catalog as meta-dataIn the stored database
    UNIVERSITYSTUDENT(Name, Student_number, Class, Major)The two records Smith and Brown

    2  Three-schema architecture and data independence

    Theory recap

    The three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) architecture

    Goal: separate the user applications from the physical database. It helps achieve three of the four characteristics of the database approach: the catalog (self-description), program-data independence, and multiple views. Schemas are defined at three levels:

    1. Internal level: the internal schema describes the physical storage structure using a physical data model: complete details of data storage and access paths.
    2. Conceptual level: the conceptual schema describes the structure of the whole database for a community of users: entities, data types, relationships, user operations, constraints; hides physical storage. Usually written in a representational model (e.g. relational), often based on a high-level conceptual design (e.g. ER).
    3. External (view) level: a number of external schemas (user views); each describes the part of the database one user group is interested in and hides the rest.
    Mappings

    The three schemas are only descriptions; the actual data exists only at the physical level. Each user group refers to its own external schema, so the DBMS must transform a request on an external schema into one on the conceptual schema, then into one on the internal schema, and reformat retrieved data back to the user’s view. These transformations are called mappings. They cost time, so some small DBMSs skip external views, but the conceptual↔\leftrightarrow↔internal mapping is always needed. Most DBMSs do not separate the levels completely, but support the architecture to some extent.

    Data independence

    Definition: Data independence

    The capacity to change the schema at one level of a database system without having to change the schema at the next higher level. Only the mapping between the two levels changes.

    Logical data independencePhysical data independence
    Change made toConceptual schemaInternal schema
    Must not affectExternal schemas and application programsConceptual schema (hence external schemas too)
    Mapping that changesExternal/conceptualConceptual/internal
    Typical changesAdd a record type or data item (expand), change constraints, remove a record type or item (reduce)Reorganize files, add an access structure (index), change record placement, compression, splitting/merging records
    ExampleChange GRADE_REPORT (Fig. 1.2) into the redundant version of Fig. 1.6(a): the TRANSCRIPT view and its programs are unaffectedAdd an index on SECTION(Semester, Year): the query “all sections in fall 2008” is unchanged but runs faster
    DifficultyHarder to achieveEasier; exists in most DBMSs and file systems
    Why logical independence is harder

    Physical details (disk location, encoding, placement) are already hidden from applications, so changing them rarely leaks upward. Logical independence must absorb structural and constraint changes, and application programs depend directly on the structure and meaning of the data they read.

    To support multiple levels, the catalog is expanded with mapping information, and the DBMS uses extra software to apply the mappings.

    3  DBMS languages and interfaces

    Theory recap

    Languages

    LanguagePurpose
    DDL (data definition language)Used by the DBA and designers to define schemas. Where levels are not strictly separated it defines both conceptual and internal schemas. A DDL compiler processes DDL statements and stores the schema description in the catalog.
    SDL (storage definition language)Specifies the internal schema where the conceptual and internal levels are clearly separated (then the DDL defines only the conceptual schema). In today’s relational DBMSs there is no separate SDL: storage is set through parameters and commands for the DBA (SDL was in early SQL versions and removed).
    VDL (view definition language)Specifies user views and their mappings to the conceptual schema (needed for a true three-schema architecture). In most DBMSs the DDL does this; in relational DBMSs SQL defines views as results of predefined queries.
    DML (data manipulation language)Retrieval, insertion, deletion and modification of data.

    Current DBMSs use one comprehensive integrated language: SQL combines DDL, VDL and DML, plus constraint specification and schema evolution. Storage definition is kept separate for the DBA.

    Two kinds of DML

    High-level (nonprocedural)Low-level (procedural)
    GranularitySet-at-a-time (set-oriented): many records in one statementRecord-at-a-time: retrieves and processes one record at a time
    SpecifiesWhat to retrieve, not how: declarativeHow: needs loops and other programming constructs
    UseStandalone interactively, or embedded in a programMust be embedded in a general-purpose language
    ExampleSQLNetwork-model (CODASYL DBTG) DML; hierarchical DL/1
    • Host language: the general-purpose language (Java, C, …) in which DML commands are embedded.
    • Data sublanguage: the DML when embedded in a host language. (Some systems integrate both, e.g. Oracle’s PL/SQL, or C++ with extensions in object databases.)
    • Query language: a high-level DML used standalone and interactively; both its retrieval and update commands count as part of the query language.
    • Casual users use a high-level query language; programmers use the DML in embedded form; naive/parametric users use friendly interfaces.

    User-friendly interfaces

    InterfaceHow it worksTypical users
    Menu-based (Web / browsing)Lists of options lead the user through a request; pull-down menus; browsing interfaces for exploratory look-through.Casual users, Web users
    Apps for mobile devicesProgrammed interfaces with login and a limited menu (pay bills, make reservations).Naive/parametric users, customers
    Forms-basedUser fills form entries to insert data, or some entries to retrieve matching data; designed for canned transactions (SQL*Forms, Oracle Forms).Naive users
    Graphical (GUI)Schema shown as a diagram; query specified by manipulating the diagram; uses menus and forms.Casual users
    Natural languageAccepts requests in English etc.; uses its own schema and a dictionary to build a high-level query, or starts a clarifying dialogue.Casual users
    Keyword-based searchLike Web search engines: keywords matched with indexes and ranking functions.Casual users
    Speech input/outputLimited vocabularies (telephone directory, flight status, card accounts).Naive users, customers
    Parametric-user interfacesSmall set of abbreviated commands / function keys to minimize keystrokes.Bank tellers, parametric users
    DBA interfacesPrivileged commands: create accounts, set parameters, grant authorization, change schema, reorganize storage.DBA staff

    4  The database system environment

    Theory recap

    DBMS component modules (Figure 2.3)

    • The database and catalog live on disk; the OS schedules disk I/O, but many DBMSs have their own buffer management. The stored data manager controls access to everything on disk (data and catalog).
    • DDL compiler: processes schema definitions, stores meta-data in the catalog (file names and sizes, data-item names and types, storage details, mappings between schemas, constraints, statistics).
    • Query compiler: parses and validates interactive queries into an internal form.
    • Query optimizer: rearranges/reorders operations, removes redundancies, chooses efficient algorithms using catalog statistics; generates executable code.
    • Precompiler: extracts DML commands from a host-language program; the DML compiler compiles them to object code; the rest goes to the host-language compiler; linked together they form a canned transaction that parametric users run repeatedly with parameters.
    • Runtime database processor: executes privileged commands, query plans and canned transactions; works with the catalog (may update statistics) and the stored data manager; handles buffers. Concurrency control and backup/recovery are integrated with it for transaction management.
    • The DBMS interacts with the operating system, compilers for host languages, application servers and client programs over the network, and communications software.

    Database system utilities

    • Loading: load existing data files (text, sequential) into the database, reformatting from a source to a target format; conversion tools for moving data between DBMSs.
    • Backup: dump the database to tape/mass storage for recovery after catastrophic disk failure; incremental backup records only changes (more complex, saves space).
    • Database storage reorganization: reorganize files into different organizations and create new access paths.
    • Performance monitoring: usage statistics for the DBA (reorganize files? add/drop indexes?).
    • Others: sorting, data compression, monitoring user access, network interfacing.

    Tools, environments, communications

    CASE tools for design; an expanded data dictionary / information repository (also stores design decisions, usage standards, program descriptions, user information; accessed mainly by users, whereas the catalog is accessed mainly by the DBMS software); application development environments (PowerBuilder, JBuilder); communications software (a DBMS integrated with data communications is a DB/DC system).

    5  Centralized and client/server architectures

    Theory recap

    Centralized DBMS

    All DBMS functionality, application program execution and user-interface processing run on one machine (originally a mainframe; users had display-only terminals). Later PCs replaced terminals but were used like terminals.

    Basic client/server

    Specialized servers (file, print, Web, e-mail, DBMS server) provide services to many clients. A client is a user machine with user-interface capabilities and local processing; when it needs extra functionality (e.g. database access) it connects to a server. A server is hardware + software providing services (file access, printing, archiving, database access). Some machines are client-only, some server-only, some both.

    Two-tier client/server

    The user interface and application programs moved to the client; query and transaction processing (SQL) stays on the server, called a query server, transaction server or SQL server. The client connects through a standard API: ODBC (Open Database Connectivity) or JDBC for Java; one client can connect to several RDBMSs. Advantages: simplicity and seamless compatibility with existing systems. Two systems hold the software components, hence “two-tier”.

    Three-tier and nnn-tier (Web applications)

    Adds an intermediate layer, the application server or Web server, between client and database server. It runs application programs and stores business rules (procedures, constraints); can improve security by checking a client’s credentials before forwarding requests; sends queries to the database server and passes (partially) processed data back, and can format results into dynamic Web pages. The three tiers: user interface (presentation layer), application rules (business logic layer), data access (database services layer). Clients are typically PCs or mobile devices with Web browsers.

    nnn-tier (nnn = 4 or 5): the business logic layer is split further. Advantages: any tier can run on an appropriate processor or OS platform and be handled independently; ERP/CRM vendors use a middleware layer so front-end modules can talk to many back-end databases. Encryption lets sensitive data travel to clients more safely.

    6  Classification of DBMSs

    Theory recap
    CriterionClasses
    Data model (main criterion)Relational (SQL systems); object; object-relational; NOSQL / big data (key-value, document (JSON), graph, column-based); native XML; legacy hierarchical and network.
    Number of usersSingle-user (mostly PCs) vs. multiuser (most DBMSs).
    Number of sitesCentralized: data at a single site (may still serve many users). Distributed (DDBMS): data and software over many sites; homogeneous (same DBMS everywhere) vs. heterogeneous; federated (multidatabase) systems loosely couple autonomous preexisting DBMSs via middleware.
    CostOpen source (MySQL, PostgreSQL), cheap personal versions, up to systems costing millions a year; site licences vs. per-user/seat licences.
    Access path optionsE.g. DBMSs based on inverted file structures.
    PurposeGeneral purpose vs. special purpose (built for performance for one application, e.g. old airline reservation and telephone directory OLTP systems).
    ModelHow it represents data
    RelationalA collection of tables (each can be stored as a separate file); high-level query language SQL; limited user views.
    ObjectObjects, their properties and operations; objects with the same structure and behaviour form a class; classes organized in hierarchies (acyclic graphs); operations are methods. Relational systems extended with these are object-relational.
    XMLHierarchical tree structures; data as elements with tags, nested into complex trees; combines database concepts with document models; a standard for exchanging data on the Web. Conceptually like the object model, different terminology.
    Key-value / document / graph / columnKey →\to→ value with very fast access by key / JSON documents resembling complex objects / nodes and directed edges / columns clustered on disk pages with multiple versions.
    Network (CODASYL DBTG)Record types plus a limited 1:N relationship called a set type (pointer-linked); record-at-a-time DML embedded in a host language (COBOL extension, 1971 DBTG report).
    HierarchicalHierarchical tree structures of related records; no standard language; IMS with DML DL/1 dominated 1965–1985.

    7  The ER model: essentials

    Theory recap

    Where the ER model sits: phases of database design (Figure 3.1)

    PhaseOutput
    Requirements collection and analysisDesigners interview prospective users. Result: a concisely written set of users’ requirements: data requirements and, in parallel, functional requirements (user-defined operations / transactions, retrievals and updates).
    Conceptual designConceptual schema in a high-level data model (ER): entity types, relationships, constraints; no implementation details; DBMS-independent.
    Functional analysisHigh-level transaction specifications (checked against the conceptual schema).
    Logical design (data model mapping)Database schema in the implementation data model of the DBMS (e.g. relational); DBMS-specific; often automated.
    Physical designInternal schema: storage structures, file organizations, indexes, access paths. In parallel: application programs (transaction implementation).
    Past-paper MCQ

    “What does the requirements-analysis phase produce?” ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ a written specification of the users’ data requirements (plus functional requirements). It does not produce the conceptual schema (that is conceptual design), the relational schema (logical design) or the internal schema (physical design).

    Entities and attributes

    Definition: Entity, attribute

    An entity is a thing or object in the real world with an independent existence: physical (a person, car, employee) or conceptual (a company, job, course). Each entity has attributes: the particular properties that describe it (an EMPLOYEE’s name, age, address, salary).

    KindMeaningExample / notation
    Simple (atomic) vs. compositeComposite attributes divide into smaller parts with independent meanings; can form a hierarchy; value = concatenation of components. Use composite only if users refer to the parts.Address( Street_address( Number, Street, Apt_no), City, State, Zip); Name(Fname, Minit, Lname). Components hang off the composite oval.
    Single-valued vs. multivaluedA set of values for one entity; may have lower/upper bounds.Car Colors (1–2 values), College_degrees, DEPARTMENT Locations. Double oval.
    Stored vs. derivedA derived value can be computed from other attributes or related entities.Age from Birth_date; Number_of_employees by counting. Dashed oval.
    NULLSpecial value when an entity has no applicable value, or the value is unknown.Not applicable: Apartment_number of a house. Unknown: missing (Height exists but not recorded) or not known whether it exists (Home_phone).
    ComplexArbitrary nesting of composite ( ) and multivalued { } attributes.{Address_phone( {Phone(Area_code, Phone_number)}, Address(…) )}

    Entity types, entity sets, keys, value sets

    • Entity type: a collection of entities that have the same attributes; described by its name and attributes. It is the schema / intension.
    • Entity set (collection): all entities of that type in the database at a point in time; the extension. Usually given the same name (EMPLOYEE means both).
    • Key attribute: values distinct for each entity in every entity set of the type (a constraint on all states, not a property of one state). Shown underlined. A composite key (e.g. Registration(Number, State) of CAR) must be minimal. An entity type can have several keys (CAR: Vehicle_id and Registration, each underlined separately). The ER model has no primary-key concept; one is chosen at mapping time. An entity type with no key is weak.
    • Value set (domain): the set of values each simple attribute may take (Age of EMPLOYEE: integers 16–70). Not shown in basic ER diagrams. Formally A:E→P(V)A : E \to \mathcal{P}(V)A:E→P(V); NULL is the empty set; single-valued means A(e)A(e)A(e) is a singleton.

    Relationship types

    Definition: Relationship type, set, instance

    A relationship type RRR among entity types E1,…,EnE_1,\dots,E_nE1​,…,En​ defines a relationship set: a set of relationship instances ri=(e1,…,en)r_i = (e_1,\dots,e_n)ri​=(e1​,…,en​) with each ej∈Eje_j \in E_jej​∈Ej​. So R⊆E1×⋯×EnR \subseteq E_1\times\cdots\times E_nR⊆E1​×⋯×En​. Each EjE_jEj​ participates in RRR. Drawn as a diamond joined to the entity boxes.

    • Degree: number of participating entity types. Binary (2, e.g. WORKS_FOR), ternary (3, e.g. SUPPLY(SUPPLIER, PART, PROJECT)).
    • Relationships as attributes: a binary relationship can be seen as a reference attribute (Department of EMPLOYEE, or the multivalued Employees of DEPARTMENT); in the ER model such references should be drawn as relationships, and the attribute removed.
    • Role names: the role an entity plays in each instance (employee/worker, department/employer). Essential in recursive (self-referencing) relationships, where one entity type participates more than once in different roles: SUPERVISION relates EMPLOYEE as supervisor and as supervisee.

    Structural constraints on binary relationships

    Cardinality ratioParticipation
    SpecifiesMaximum number of relationship instances an entity can participate inMinimum: whether an entity’s existence depends on being related (minimum cardinality)
    Values1:1, 1:N, N:1, M:NTotal (existence dependency) or partial
    Notation1, N, M on the linesTotal: double line; partial: single line
    COMPANYMANAGES 1:1, WORKS_FOR 1:N (DEPARTMENT:EMPLOYEE), WORKS_ON M:NEvery employee works for a department: total; not every employee manages one: partial

    Cardinality ratio + participation together are the structural constraints of a relationship type.

    Definition: (min,max) notation

    Associate a pair (min⁡,max⁡)(\min,\max)(min,max) with each participation of entity type EEE in RRR, 0≤min⁡≤max⁡0 \le \min \le \max0≤min≤max, max⁡≥1\max \ge 1max≥1: each entity e∈Ee \in Ee∈E participates in at least min and at most max instances of RRR at any time. min⁡=0\min = 0min=0 means partial, min⁡>0\min > 0min>0 total. More precise than 1:N plus single/double lines, and usable for higher degrees.

    (min,max) is written on the opposite side from 1/N

    In the book’s (Abrial) notation the pair next to EEE describes EEE’s own participation. For WORKS_FOR: EMPLOYEE side (1,1) (each employee works for exactly one department), DEPARTMENT side (4,N) (each department has at least 4 employees). In the 1:N notation the “N” sits next to EMPLOYEE and the “1” next to DEPARTMENT: the max of the (min,max) on one side is the ratio number written on the other side. UML puts (min,max) on the opposite ends; whichever you use, be consistent (the GA2 rubric accepts either if used throughout).

    Attributes of relationship types

    Relationships can have attributes: Hours of WORKS_ON, Start_date of MANAGES.

    • 1:1: the attribute may migrate to either participant (Start_date to EMPLOYEE or DEPARTMENT).
    • 1:N: it may migrate only to the N-side entity (Start_date of WORKS_FOR to EMPLOYEE).
    • M:N: attributes determined by the combination of entities must stay on the relationship (Hours).

    Weak entity types

    • Weak entity type: has no key attribute of its own; entities are identified by being related to an identifying (owner) entity type through the identifying relationship, in combination with a partial key (discriminator), e.g. DEPENDENT identified by its EMPLOYEE plus dependent Name. Strong = regular entity types with a key.
    • A weak entity type always has total participation in its identifying relationship. But not every existence dependency gives a weak entity: DRIVER_LICENSE needs a PERSON but has its own key (License_number).
    • Notation: double rectangle, double diamond, partial key dashed underline.
    • Alternative: model as a multivalued composite attribute (Dependents of EMPLOYEE); prefer the weak entity if it takes part in other relationships. Owners may themselves be weak; identifying relationships may have degree >2>2>2.

    ER notation summary (Figure 3.14)

    The COMPANY database (Figures 3.2 / 3.15): main points

    Requirements: departments (unique name and number, a manager with start date, several locations); projects (unique name and number, one location, controlled by a department); employees (Ssn, name, address, salary, sex, birth date; one department; several projects with hours per week; a direct supervisor); dependents (first name, sex, birth date, relationship) for insurance.

    RelationshipRatio(min,max)Participation and notes
    MANAGES (EMP–DEPT)1:1EMP (0,1), DEPT (1,1)EMP partial; DEPT total (a department always has a manager). Attribute Start_date.
    WORKS_FOR (DEPT–EMP)1:NEMP (1,1), DEPT (4,N)Both total. (4,N): at least 4 employees per department (Fig. 3.15).
    CONTROLS (DEPT–PROJ)1:NDEPT (0,N), PROJ (1,1)PROJECT total, DEPARTMENT partial.
    SUPERVISION (EMP–EMP)1:Nsupervisor (0,N), supervisee (0,1)Recursive, with role names; both partial.
    WORKS_ON (EMP–PROJ)M:NEMP (1,N), PROJ (1,N)Both total. Attribute Hours (must stay on the relationship).
    DEPENDENTS_OF (EMP–DEPENDENT)1:NEMP (0,N), DEPENDENT (1,1)Identifying relationship of weak DEPENDENT (partial key Name); EMP partial, DEPENDENT total.

    Design notes: the initial design (Figure 3.8) had reference attributes (Manager, Controlling_department, Department, Supervisor, Works_on, Employee); each was refined into a relationship and the attribute was removed, keeping redundancy minimal. Names: entity types singular and uppercase, relationship types uppercase, attributes capitalized, roles lowercase; nouns suggest entity types, verbs suggest relationship types. Concepts may be refined attribute →\to→ relationship, attribute →\to→ entity type (Department shared by several types), or entity type →\to→ attribute.

    Worked example from Moodle: the GA2 key (an EER model of the ER model itself)

    GA2 asked for a (min,max) EER diagram whose miniworld is the ER model’s own vocabulary. The key builds it in ten steps, one per sentence of the definitions; its main ideas revise this section:

    • Entity described by Attribute: (1,N) on both sides (an entity has at least one attribute; one attribute, e.g. pincode, can describe many entities).
    • Attribute is specialized three times, each disjoint (d): Simple vs. Composite, Single-valued vs. Multivalued, Stored vs. Derived; the three classifications overlap (o) with each other (an attribute can be simple, single-valued and stored at once). “Accepts NULL” is an attribute of every Attribute; Value set is attached to the multivalued case.
    • Composite attribute consists of Attribute with (2,N) on the composite side (at least two components); a component can belong to 0..N composites; Component count is a derived attribute.
    • Entity type (key: Name) has instances Entity: an entity belongs to exactly one type (1,1).
    • Strong entity type has key attribute Key attribute (a subclass of Attribute).
    • Relationship type joins entity types (1,N on each line) and may have its own attributes; Binary relationship type joins exactly two.
    • Participation and Cardinality constraint are a disjoint pair of special attributes, each a composite (min, max).
    • Weak entity type has partial key Partial key attribute; it is linked to its Strong entity type through the Identifying relationship type with (1,1) on the weak side (exactly one owner) and (0,N) on the owner side.
    • Specialization: recursive has subclass on Entity type (a subclass has at most one superclass here, (0,1)); Generalization combines (2,N) strong entity types into one superclass.
    What GA2’s rubric rewarded in any ER/EER diagram

    Major mistakes (grade C): a strong entity with no underlined key, or a weak entity with no partial key; any relationship end without a (min,max) pair (writing 1:N, N or 1 instead); logical flaws such as min >>> max, a weak entity with min 0 on its identifying relationship, a weak entity with no identifying relationship, d/o contradicting the diagram, a relationship with one participant and no ring. Minor mistakes: no multivalued or composite attribute anywhere; wrong notation (weak entity not double box, identifying relationship not double diamond, partial key solid instead of dashed, derived not dashed); no written assumptions. Naming and layout are not penalized.

    8  Quick MCQ-style checks

    Theory recap

    Past quizzes asked MCQs on schema vs. instance, the three-schema architecture, data models, and what requirements analysis produces. Decide true or false, then check.

    StatementT/FWhy
    1The database schema changes every time a record is inserted.FThe state changes; the schema changes rarely (schema evolution).
    2The schema is called the intension and a state the extension.TSection 2.1.2.
    3Immediately after the schema is defined, the database is in the empty state.TInitial state comes when data is first loaded.
    4A data model is the description of one particular database.FIt is a collection of concepts for describing structure (+ operations, constraints); one database’s description is its schema.
    5The relational model is a high-level conceptual data model.FIt is representational (implementation, record-based); ER is conceptual.
    6In the three-schema architecture, the conceptual schema describes the physical storage structures.FThat is the internal schema; the conceptual schema describes the whole database for all users and hides storage.
    7Actual data is stored only at the internal (physical) level.TThe three schemas are only descriptions.
    8Adding an index without changing applications or the conceptual schema shows logical data independence.FPhysical data independence.
    9Logical data independence is harder to achieve than physical.TApplications depend on structure and constraints.
    10SQL is a procedural, record-at-a-time DML.FNonprocedural (declarative), set-at-a-time.
    11The requirements-analysis phase produces the conceptual schema.FIt produces a written set of users’ data (and functional) requirements; conceptual design produces the conceptual schema.
    12A weak entity type always has total participation in its identifying relationship.TIt cannot be identified without its owner.
    13Every entity with an existence dependency is weak.FDRIVER_LICENSE depends on PERSON but has its own key.
    14In a 1:N relationship, a relationship attribute can be migrated to the 1-side entity.FOnly to the N-side.

    Textbook exercises

    2.1Define the termsE&N Ex. 2.1 · p. 55

    Define the following terms: data model, database schema, database state, internal schema, conceptual schema, external schema, data independence, DDL, DML, SDL, VDL, query language, host language, data sublanguage, database utility, catalog, client/server architecture, three-tier architecture, and n-tier architecture.

    Solution · written for this guide
    TermDefinition (with an example)
    Data modelA collection of concepts used to describe the structure of a database (data types, relationships, constraints), usually with basic operations for retrieval and update (e.g. the relational model, the ER model).
    Database schemaThe description of the database, specified at design time and rarely changed (e.g. STUDENT(Name, Student_number, Class, Major) in Figure 2.1).
    Database stateThe data in the database at a particular moment; the current set of instances; changes on every update (e.g. the records Smith and Brown).
    Internal schemaSchema at the internal level: physical storage structures, complete storage details and access paths, described with a physical data model.
    Conceptual schemaSchema at the conceptual level: structure of the whole database for a community of users (entities, types, relationships, operations, constraints), hiding storage details.
    External schemaA user view: the part of the database one user group is interested in, hiding the rest (e.g. TRANSCRIPT).
    Data independenceThe capacity to change the schema at one level without changing the schema at the next higher level; only the mapping changes (logical and physical).
    DDLData definition language: used by the DBA/designers to define (conceptual, and where no separation, also internal) schemas; compiled into the catalog.
    DMLData manipulation language: retrieval, insertion, deletion and modification of data.
    SDLStorage definition language: specifies the internal schema when the conceptual and internal levels are separated.
    VDLView definition language: specifies user views (external schemas) and their mappings to the conceptual schema.
    Query languageA high-level DML used standalone and interactively (e.g. SQL typed at a prompt).
    Host languageA general-purpose programming language (Java, C, …) in which DML statements are embedded.
    Data sublanguageThe DML when it is embedded in a host language.
    Database utilityA DBMS-supplied program that helps the DBA manage the system: loading, backup, storage reorganization, performance monitoring, sorting, compression.
    CatalogThe part of the DBMS that stores meta-data: schema descriptions, data types, storage details, mappings, constraints, statistics.
    Client/server architectureFunctionality is split between client modules (user interface, applications, on user machines) and server modules that provide services (data storage, access, query processing) over a network.
    Three-tier architectureClient (presentation: GUI, browser) ↔\leftrightarrow↔ application/Web server (business logic, rules, security checks) ↔\leftrightarrow↔ database server (DBMS).
    nnn-tier architectureGeneralizes three-tier by splitting layers (usually the business logic) further, nnn = 4 or 5; each tier can run on its own platform and be managed independently.
    2.2Categories of data modelsE&N Ex. 2.2 · p. 55

    Discuss the main categories of data models. What are the basic differences among the relational model, the object model, and the XML model?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Categories (by the concepts they use)

    1. High-level / conceptual: close to how users perceive data; concepts are entities, attributes, relationships. Example: the ER and EER models. Used for conceptual design.
    2. Representational / implementation: understandable by users yet close to storage organization and implementable directly; record-based. Examples: relational (dominant), network and hierarchical (legacy); the object model as a higher-level implementation model.
    3. Low-level / physical: how data is stored as files: record formats, orderings, access paths (indexes, hashing). For specialists.
    4. Self-describing: the description is stored with the data values (XML, key-value and NOSQL systems).

    Relational vs. object vs. XML

    RelationalObjectXML
    StructureFlat tables (relations) of rows; each table may be a fileObjects with properties grouped into classes; classes in hierarchies (inheritance)Hierarchical tree of nested elements marked with tags
    BehaviourData only (stored procedures added)Operations (methods) defined with the classNone; data only
    RelationshipsBy matching values (foreign keys)Object references / identityNesting (parent-child) and references
    SchemaSeparate schema in the catalogClass definitionsSelf-describing: tags travel with the data
    LanguageSQL, high-level declarativeOO language integration (ODMG)XPath/XQuery
    Main useTraditional business databasesComplex objects (CAD, multimedia)Data exchange on the Web
    Answer

    Conceptual, representational (implementation) and physical models (plus self-describing ones). Relational = tables of records related by values; object = classes of objects with attributes and methods, organized in hierarchies; XML = self-describing hierarchical trees of tagged elements, used mainly for exchanging data.

    2.3Schema vs. stateE&N Ex. 2.3 · p. 55

    What is the difference between a database schema and a database state?

    Solution · written for this guide
    • The database schema is the description of the database: the record types, data items, data types and constraints. It is specified during design (in the DDL), stored in the catalog as meta-data, and is not expected to change frequently (changes are schema evolution). Also called the intension.
    • The database state (snapshot) is the actual data in the database at a particular moment: the current set of instances of every schema construct. It changes every time a record is inserted, deleted or modified. Also called the extension.

    Life cycle: defining the schema gives the empty state; loading data gives the initial state; each update gives a new current state. Many states correspond to one schema, and the DBMS must ensure every state is valid (satisfies the schema’s structure and constraints).

    UNIVERSITY

    Schema: STUDENT(Name, Student_number, Class, Major), Class an integer 1–5. State: {(Smith, 17, 1, CS), (Brown, 8, 2, CS)}. “Change Smith’s class to 2” changes the state, not the schema. “Add Date_of_birth to STUDENT” changes the schema (schema evolution).

    Answer

    Schema = description (intension), stable; state = the data at an instant (extension), changes with every update.

    2.4Three-schema architectureE&N Ex. 2.4 · p. 55★ Must-do

    Describe the three-schema architecture. Why do we need mappings among schema levels? How do different schema definition languages support this architecture?

    Solution · written for this guide

    1. The architecture

    The three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) architecture separates user applications from the physical database by defining schemas at three levels:

    1. Internal level / internal schema: physical storage structure, described with a physical data model: complete storage details and access paths (e.g. STUDENT stored as fixed-length records, an index on Student_number).
    2. Conceptual level / conceptual schema: the structure of the whole database for all users: entities, data types, relationships, user operations and constraints; hides storage. Usually in a representational model (e.g. the five relations of Figure 2.1), often designed first in ER.
    3. External (view) level / external schemas: one per user group; each shows only the part of the database the group needs and hides the rest (e.g. TRANSCRIPT for the transcript office, COURSE_PREREQUISITES for registration).

    Most DBMSs do not separate the three levels completely but support the architecture to some extent.

    2. Why mappings are needed

    The three schemas are only descriptions: the data exists only at the physical level. A user group works in terms of its external schema, so the DBMS must

    • transform a request on an external schema into a request on the conceptual schema (external/conceptual mapping), then into a request on the internal schema (conceptual/internal mapping), to be processed on the stored database; and
    • for a retrieval, reformat the extracted data back to match the user’s external view.

    Mappings also deliver data independence: when a lower-level schema changes, only the mapping is changed and the higher-level schema (and the programs using it) stay the same. The mapping information is stored in the catalog. Mappings cost time, so some small DBMSs do not support external views, but the conceptual/internal mapping is always needed.

    3. How schema definition languages support it

    LanguageLevel it definesNotes
    SDLInternal schemaUsed where the conceptual and internal levels are clearly separated; in today’s RDBMSs replaced by DBA storage parameters and commands (indexes, file placement).
    DDLConceptual schemaCompiled by the DDL compiler into the catalog; where levels are not separated, also defines the internal schema.
    VDLExternal schemasDefines user views and their mapping to the conceptual schema; in most DBMSs the DDL plays this role.

    The conceptual/internal mapping may be specified in either the DDL or the SDL. In relational systems SQL is a single integrated language acting as DDL (CREATE TABLE), VDL (CREATE VIEW) and DML; storage definition (SDL) was removed from SQL and is left to DBA-specific commands.

    SQL in the three roles (UNIVERSITY)
    CREATE TABLE STUDENT (Name VARCHAR(30), Student_number CHAR(4) PRIMARY KEY,
                      Class INT, Major CHAR(4));                        -- DDL: conceptual
CREATE VIEW TRANSCRIPT AS
  SELECT S.Name, SE.Course_number, G.Grade, SE.Semester, SE.Year, SE.Section_identifier
  FROM STUDENT S, GRADE_REPORT G, SECTION SE
  WHERE S.Student_number = G.Student_number
    AND G.Section_identifier = SE.Section_identifier;                   -- VDL: external
CREATE INDEX Sect_term ON SECTION (Semester, Year);    -- storage tuning (SDL role, DBA command)
    What the grader checks

    Full marks need all three parts: (i) the three levels with what each describes (a diagram helps); (ii) mappings = transforming requests downward and results upward, and their link to data independence; (iii) SDL →\to→ internal, DDL →\to→ conceptual, VDL →\to→ external, noting that in practice SQL/DDL covers several roles. Common loss: describing the conceptual schema as “the ER diagram” only, or calling the internal schema “the data”.

    2.5Logical vs. physical data independenceE&N Ex. 2.5 · p. 55★ Must-do

    What is the difference between logical data independence and physical data independence? Which one is harder to achieve? Why?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Definitions

    Data independence: the capacity to change the schema at one level without having to change the schema at the next higher level; only the mapping between the two levels changes.

    • Logical data independence: the capacity to change the conceptual schema without having to change the external schemas or the application programs. Only the external/conceptual mapping (view definitions) changes.
    • Physical data independence: the capacity to change the internal schema without having to change the conceptual schema (and hence the external schemas). Only the conceptual/internal mapping changes.

    Examples (UNIVERSITY)

    • Logical: add a data item Birth_date to STUDENT, add a new record type, change a constraint, or replace GRADE_REPORT by the version of Figure 1.6(a) with redundant Student_name and Course_number. The TRANSCRIPT view and the programs that use it must keep working; only the view’s mapping is rewritten. Removing a record type must not affect external schemas that use only the remaining data.
    • Physical: add an index on SECTION(Semester, Year), reorganize files, change record placement or compression. The query “list all sections offered in fall 2008” is unchanged; it runs faster.
    LogicalPhysical
    Schema changedConceptualInternal
    ProtectedExternal schemas, application programsConceptual schema (and above)
    Mapping changedExternal/conceptualConceptual/internal
    Kind of changeStructure and constraints (add/remove record types, data items, constraints)Storage (indexes, file organization, placement, encoding)
    DifficultyHarderEasier; common in most DBMSs

    Which is harder, and why

    Logical data independence is harder to achieve.

    • Physical details (exact disk location, storage encoding, placement, compression, splitting and merging of records) are already hidden from users and programs in most DBMSs and even file systems, so changing them rarely affects anything above the conceptual level.
    • Logical independence must let the structure and constraints of the data change without affecting application programs, which are written against that structure and meaning. A conceptual change can remove or reshape data a program relies on, or change what a view can express (for example, views over changed structure may no longer be updatable), so the mapping cannot always hide it.
    Answer

    Logical: change the conceptual schema without changing external schemas/programs. Physical: change the internal schema without changing the conceptual schema. Logical data independence is harder, because programs depend directly on the logical structure and constraints, whereas physical storage details are already hidden from them.

    What the grader checks

    Expect: both definitions naming the two levels involved and what must not change; one example each; “logical is harder” with a reason (programs depend on structure/meaning; physical details already hidden). Swapping the two definitions is the most common error.

    10  Chapter 2 exercise

    Textbook exercises

    2.14Architecture for a Web airline-reservation systemE&N Ex. 2.14 · p. 56

    If you were designing a Web-based system to make airline reservations and sell airline tickets, which DBMS architecture would you choose from Section 2.5? Why? Why would the other architectures not be a good choice?

    Solution · written for this guide

    Assumptions (stated and justified)

    1. Customers use ordinary Web browsers or mobile apps over the Internet; travel agents and airline staff also use the system. Why: the question says “Web-based” and “sell tickets”.
    2. There are very many concurrent users updating the same seat inventory, and payments are involved. Why: this is the book’s standard example of an OLTP application (Section 1.3.4).

    Choice: three-tier (or nnn-tier) client/server architecture (Section 2.5.4)

    TierRole in the airline system
    Client (presentation layer)Web browser or mobile app: search flights, choose seats, enter passenger and payment details, display itineraries and e-tickets. No DBMS software needed on the client.
    Application / Web server (business logic)Runs the reservation programs and business rules: fare calculation, seat availability, overbooking limits, cancellation and refund policy, payment processing; checks the customer’s credentials before forwarding requests; builds dynamic Web pages from query results.
    Database server (data services)DBMS holding flights, seats, fares, bookings, customers, payments; provides concurrency control (no seat sold twice), recovery and atomic transactions.

    Why three-tier fits

    1. Web access by thin clients: millions of users with only a browser. The middle tier formats results as Web pages: the Web application pattern of Section 2.5.4.
    2. Security: customers never connect to the database directly; the application server authenticates them and sends only validated requests. Sensitive data (payment details) can be encrypted. The database server can sit behind a firewall.
    3. Business rules in one place: fares and booking rules change often; changing them on the application server updates every client at once.
    4. Scalability and concurrency: application servers can be replicated to handle load, while the database server enforces concurrency control on shared seat inventory.
    5. Integration: the middle tier can also talk to payment gateways and other airlines’ or agents’ systems. If this grows, the business layer can be split further into an nnn-tier design (separate pricing, payment and booking services), each on its own platform.

    Why not the others

    • Centralized architecture: all processing (DBMS, applications, user interface) on one machine, with users on terminals. It does not suit the Web: users are remote PCs and phones, one machine becomes a performance bottleneck and single point of failure, and it does not use the client’s processing power.
    • Two-tier client/server: application programs and UI run on the client, which connects directly to the DBMS through ODBC/JDBC. For a public Web system this means (i) DBMS client software/drivers and application code on every user’s machine, which is impossible to control for millions of customers; (ii) database access exposed to untrusted clients, a security risk; (iii) business rules duplicated on every client, so each change requires redeploying all clients; (iv) a database connection per client, which does not scale. Two-tier suits a controlled internal setting (for example the airline’s own office staff), not Internet ticket sales.
    Answer

    A three-tier (extendable to nnn-tier) Web architecture: browser/app client, application/Web server holding business rules and security checks, and a database server. Centralized does not support distributed Web clients and does not scale; two-tier puts application logic and direct database connections on untrusted, uncontrolled clients, which is insecure, hard to maintain and does not scale.

    11  Exam cheat sheet

    Data models, schemas and states

    • Data model: a collection of concepts describing structure (types, relationships, constraints) + basic operations (+ behaviour, e.g. COMPUTE_GPA). Not one database’s description (that is its schema).
    • Categories: conceptual (entities, attributes, relationships: ER, EER); representational = record-based (relational; network, hierarchical; object); physical (record formats, orderings, access paths); self-describing (XML, key-value, NOSQL).
    • Schema: the description, set at design time, rarely changes; a schema diagram shows record types and item names only (no types, relationships, most constraints).
    • State (snapshot): data at one moment; changes on every update. Empty →\to→ initial (first load) →\to→ current; the DBMS keeps every state valid.
    • Intension = schema (in catalog), extension = state. Schema evolution: schema change when requirements change (add Date_of_birth).

    Three-schema architecture and data independence

    • Goal: separate user applications from the physical database (catalog, program-data independence, views).
    • Internal: physical storage and access paths. Conceptual: the whole database for all users (entities, types, relationships, operations, constraints), hides storage. External: one view per user group, rest hidden (TRANSCRIPT).
    • Mappings: data exists only at the internal level, so the DBMS transforms requests external →\to→ conceptual →\to→ internal and reformats results back up. Stored in the catalog; conceptual/internal always needed.
    • Data independence: change one level’s schema without changing the next higher one; only the mapping changes.
    LogicalPhysical
    ChangeConceptual schemaInternal schema
    SafeExternal schemas, programsConceptual (and above)
    MappingExternal/conceptualConceptual/internal
    ExampleAdd Birth_date; TRANSCRIPT unchangedIndex on SECTION(Semester, Year)
    DifficultyHarder: programs depend on structureEasier: storage already hidden

    DBMS languages and interfaces

    • DDL →\to→ conceptual (also internal if not separated), compiled into the catalog; SDL →\to→ internal (now DBA commands); VDL →\to→ external views + mappings; DML: retrieve, insert, delete, modify. SQL integrates DDL, VDL, DML.
    • High-level DML: declarative, set-at-a-time, what (SQL). Low-level: procedural, record-at-a-time, how, must be embedded (CODASYL, DL/1).
    • Host language embeds DML = data sublanguage; standalone interactive DML = query language.
    • Interfaces: menu/browsing, mobile apps, forms (canned), GUI, natural language, keyword, speech, parametric (function keys), DBA (privileged).

    System environment

    • Modules: DDL compiler →\to→ catalog; query compiler →\to→ query optimizer (uses catalog statistics); precompiler splits DML (DML compiler) from host code, linked into canned transactions; runtime DB processor executes them with concurrency control and backup/recovery; stored data manager controls disk.
    • Catalog (meta-data incl. mappings, statistics) serves the DBMS; data dictionary serves users.
    • Utilities: loading, backup (incremental), storage reorganization, performance monitoring.

    Architectures and classification

    • Centralized: everything on one machine, users on terminals.
    • Two-tier: UI + apps on the client; query/transaction processing on the SQL server; via ODBC/JDBC. Simple, compatible.
    • Three-tier: client (presentation) ↔\leftrightarrow↔ application/Web server (business rules, credential checks, Web pages) ↔\leftrightarrow↔ database server. nnn-tier: logic split further, n=4,5n=4,5n=4,5.
    • Web airline (2.14): three/nnn-tier: thin clients, security, rules in one place, scales. Centralized: no remote clients, bottleneck. Two-tier: code + DB connections on untrusted clients, does not scale.
    • Classify by: data model (main), users (single/multi), sites (centralized / distributed: homogeneous, heterogeneous, federated), cost, access paths, purpose (general/special).
    • Relational: tables linked by values. Object: classes with methods, hierarchies. XML: self-describing tagged tree. Network: 1:N set types. Hierarchical: trees (IMS, DL/1).

    ER model: design phases, entities, attributes

    • Phases: requirements analysis →\to→ written data (+ functional) requirements; conceptual design →\to→ ER schema; functional analysis →\to→ transaction specs; logical design →\to→ relational schema; physical design →\to→ internal schema.
    • Entity: thing with independent existence (person; course). Attributes describe it.
    • Composite (Address(Street_address(Number, Street, Apt_no), City, State, Zip)) vs. simple; multivalued (double oval: Colors, Locations); derived (dashed oval: Age, Number_of_employees). Complex: nested ( ) and { }.
    • NULL: not applicable (Apartment_number of a house) or unknown.
    • Entity type = intension; entity set = extension.
    • Key: unique in every state, underlined, minimal; several allowed (CAR: Vehicle_id, Registration). No primary key in ER. No key ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ weak. Value set: domain (Age 16–70), not drawn.

    ER model: relationships

    • Relationship type: R⊆E1×⋯×EnR \subseteq E_1 \times \dots \times E_nR⊆E1​×⋯×En​, diamond; degree binary, ternary. Reference attributes →\to→ draw as relationships. Role names needed in recursive ones (SUPERVISION).
    • Cardinality ratio = max (1:1, 1:N, M:N). Participation = min: total (double line) or partial. Together: structural constraints.
    • (min,max): 0≤min⁡≤max⁡0 \le \min \le \max0≤min≤max, max⁡≥1\max \ge 1max≥1; min =0=0=0 partial, >0>0>0 total. Beside EEE = EEE’s own participation: WORKS_FOR EMPLOYEE (1,1), DEPT (4,N); 1:N puts N beside EMPLOYEE.
    • Relationship attributes: 1:1 either side; 1:N only N-side; M:N stays (Hours of WORKS_ON).
    • Weak entity: no own key; owner + identifying relationship + partial key (DEPENDENT Name); always total; double box, double diamond, dashed underline. DRIVER_LICENSE is existence-dependent but not weak.
    COMPANY(min,max)
    MANAGES (Start_date)1:1EMP (0,1), DEPT (1,1)
    WORKS_FOR1:NEMP (1,1), DEPT (4,N)
    CONTROLS1:NDEPT (0,N), PROJ (1,1)
    SUPERVISION1:Nsup. (0,N), sub. (0,1)
    WORKS_ON (Hours)M:NEMP (1,N), PROJ (1,N)
    DEPENDENTS_OF1:NEMP (0,N), DEP (1,1)

    Traps that cost marks

    • Data model ≠\ne= schema; relational is representational, not conceptual. Inserting changes the state, not the schema.
    • Conceptual schema hides storage; the internal one describes it. Index = physical independence; swapping logical/physical is the commonest error.
    • SQL is declarative, set-at-a-time. Requirements analysis yields written requirements, not a schema.
    • GA2 major: key not underlined, weak entity without partial key or identifying relationship, a line without a (min,max) pair, min >>> max, weak side min 000. Minor: wrong double/dashed notation, no composite or multivalued attribute, no assumptions.

    Exam moves

    • Three-schema: levels + diagram; mappings (requests down, results up) give independence; SDL/DDL/VDL per level.
    • Independence: name both levels and what must not change; one example each; logical harder + why.
    • Architecture / ER: justify the choice and reject each alternative; on diagrams state assumptions and put (min,max) on every line, consistently.
